beats.narration_text: Gavia finds loons in photos, on your own computer, and a person checks every box. This is Sai. This week's question: which animal should get the next Gavia? Not the most charismatic one. The one that passes four questions.

show.event: the ask types in under 'Hello, Sai'
three plain result lines land
'seals pass all four' lands last and holds

props.command: Gavia finds loons in photos, offline, for a person to review. Which wildlife should the next Gavia count? Check who counts it by hand today, whether a dataset lets us ship trained weights, and whether an offline app already exists.
props.runningText: checking datasets, licences and existing tools…
output: four questions: demand, data, gap, fit
camera traps and bird song: already covered
seals pass all four; Maine seabirds, three

beats.narration_text: Here are the four. Demand: is someone counting this animal by hand today, on the record? Data: is there a labelled set we're allowed to train on, and then ship the weights from? Gap: is there no installable, offline app for it yet? And fit: still photos or drone frames, turned into boxes or points, the way Gavia works.

show.event: Demand lands first
Data and Gap land as they are asked
Fit closes the grid; the caption: pass all four

beats.narration_text: Two big areas drop out first. Camera traps fail the gap question: MegaDetector, Google's SpeciesNet and the free AddaxAI app already run on your own computer. Bird song fails on data: Bird Net is excellent, but its models are licensed non-commercial, and Gavia's AGPL license can't carry that. Gavia's niche is narrower: one kind of animal in photos, counted offline, checked by a person.

show.event: the question splits: camera traps, bird song
each branch names what already exists
the resolver: Gavia's narrower niche

data.question: Camera traps and bird song: build the next Gavia there?

branches.label: Bird song

resolver.label: Gavia's niche

data.ghostText: one fails the gap question, the other fails the data question

beats.narration_text: Demand looks like this. On the Texas coast, Houston Audubon flew a drone over waterbird colonies, and going through the imagery took weeks. With computer help it took about nineteen percent of the time. One minus point one nine is point eight one: their eighty percent cut. And the computer found eighty-nine percent of the birds a biologist found, so a person still checks. That's Gavia's shape.

show.event: the assisted time typesets as 0.19 of the hand time
the 89% of birds found lands beneath

props.title: What hand review costs, and what help saves
props.note: Computer-assisted: about 19% of the time, 89% of the birds.
props.conditions: t: review time · N: birds found · Houston Audubon + Rice University (SeeBird), Audubon, 24 Sep 2026 · 0.81 rounds to their “80%”.

beats.narration_text: Now Maine's coastal islands. In twenty nineteen a survey plane photographed two hundred sixty-eight islands, and three observers went through the images, bird by bird: herring gulls, eiders, cormorants. When two or more looked at the same bird, they agreed on its species ninety-nine percent of the time. That's demand, on the record, and photos into points is Gavia's fit.

show.event: an aerial colony photo, birds as dots, is up first
herring gull, eider and cormorant arrive as they are named
all four hold while the 99% agreement is read

beats.narration_text: The data question, measured. We downloaded both releases and counted. Maine: ninety-seven thousand two hundred seventy-two birds labelled, and zero images. The NOAA Arctic seals: fourteen thousand three hundred eleven seals boxed, on forty-four thousand colour images, under a permissive licence. Points without the photos under them can't train a detector.

show.event: Maine's 97,272 labelled birds land
Maine's images released: 0
the seals: 14,311 boxed on 44,185 colour images

props.title: What each release actually contains
props.note: USGS doi:10.5066/P92SL92P (CSV + XML only) · LILA NOAA Arctic Seals 2019, CDLA-Permissive · evidence/maine_labels.py, seal_labels.py, 25 Oct 2026

beats.narration_text: Seals pass all four. Demand: on Alaska's Iliamna Lake, NOAA photographed every harbor seal it saw from a plane, then counted them from the photos. Data: open and permissive, as we just measured, and mostly ringed seals. Gap: we found no installable offline app that counts seals in photos. Fit: seals hauled out on rocks or ice, seen from above, are boxes on a photo, like loons.

New England harbor seals on rocks arrive with 'fit'

beats.narration_text: So the ranking falls out of the questions. Seals: build now, on open data. Maine's seabirds: one step first. The labels are public and the photos aren't, but the release names a contact. So the next step there is a request for the imagery, not code.

show.event: both candidates start from the same four questions
they split at data
the badges land: build now, request images

beats.narration_text: So, the next Gavia: picked by four questions, not by charisma. Seals pass all four today. Maine's seabirds wait on one request for images. Camera traps and bird song are already served, so we leave them alone.

show.event: the one-page card opens
the camera-trap and seal lines fill in
'request them' closes it

artifactLines: Four questions pick the next species: demand, data, gap and fit. Charisma isn't one of them.
Camera traps already have free local tools. BirdNET's models are non-commercial, so they can't ship in AGPL Gavia.
Seals pass all four: NOAA counts them from photos, and 14,311 boxed seals are public under CDLA-Permissive.
Maine's seabirds pass three: 97,272 birds are labelled, but no images are released. Next step: request them.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Pick an animal you care about and run the four questions with an assistant: who counts it by hand today, is there a labelled set whose licence lets you ship weights, does an offline tool already exist, and do photos fit? Then open the licence page yourself and check its answer.

show.event: the handoff prompt types in under 'Your turn.'
the four checks stack as it fills
'Link every source' lands and the cursor holds
